_doc: Phase 379. One row per item where the nano-ros user API does NOT correspond
to the ROS 2 client library it mirrors. Written by hand; read by
`scripts/api-parity.py --check`, which fails on any non-matching row that has
no entry here.
Key is '<lang>:<normalized item>' exactly as the report prints it, where lang
is one of c / cpp / rust. Run the report to get the spelling; do not guess it.
verdict is one of:
divergence  we changed it and a PLATFORM CONSTRAINT is why. `why` must name
the constraint (no_std, no exceptions, no allocator, no runtime
env, single-threaded transport) -- not a preference. This is the
only sanctioned reason to differ (RFC-0036).
extension   we add it because an RTOS scenario needs it; ROS 2 has none.
declined    ROS 2 has it, we deliberately do not, with the reason.
gap         ROS 2 has it, we should too, nobody has done it. A gap is a
legitimate entry -- the point is that it is written down.
rename      the names differ and OURS is the one that should change. A
rename with no platform reason costs the drop-in claim for
nothing, so these are the campaign's work list.
This file is SEEDED, not complete: W1 shipped the correlator, W2 classifies
the rest. `--check` is deliberately not wired into `just check` until then --
a gate that fails on ~2000 rows from the day it lands is one somebody
switches off. Keys beginning with '_' are documentation and are skipped.
the `<lang>:` rows for its own lane, and `scripts/api-parity.py` merges every
shard in this directory. One agent per lane can write without a rebase
conflict against the others.

languages, because the campaign closes a feature at a time across every
language. `scripts/api-parity.py` merges every shard here, and

c:count_status_t.why: the counted-event payload. rmw declares one status struct per event (`rmw_requested_deadline_missed_status_t`, `rmw_offered_deadline_missed_status_t`, `rmw_message_lost_status_t`) that are field-identical, and rclcpp typedefs each one to its own `QOS*Info` name. Ours is a single `nros_count_status_t` (`total_count`, `total_count_change`) shared by all three, plus `nros_liveliness_changed_status_t` for the one that differs. The widths are fixed (`uint32_t`, and `uint16_t`/`int16_t` for the liveliness counters) rather than `size_t`/`int32_t`: the payload crosses the C ABI BY VALUE into a callback, so it must have one layout on a 64-bit host and a 32-bit target -- the same hand-mirrored-FFI-struct hazard issue 0160 gated. These print as ours-only because the ROS 2 originals live in `rmw`, which is outside the rclc+rcl surface this report compares.

c:node_set_qos_overrides.why: installs the baked override table on the node, once, before any entity is created. The ours-only half of `cpp:QosOverridingOptions`; the same call exists in all three languages under the same name (`nros_node_set_qos_overrides`, `Node::set_qos_overrides`, `NodeHandle::set_qos_overrides`), which is the one place this stage found our languages already agreeing. QoS overrides. rclcpp's `QosOverridingOptions` is handed to each entity's options at creation; it DECLARES `qos_overrides.<topic>.<role>.<policy>` parameters on the node, reads them back at runtime and runs a user validation callback over the result. Ours keeps the same launch-parameter spelling but resolves it at BUILD time: the deploy plan lowers each override into a `&'static [QosOverride]` table, the entry installs it once with `set_qos_overrides` before any entity exists, and the node folds the matching `(topic, role)` rows into the profile inside `create_publisher`/`create_subscription` -- setup-time, before the backend-compat check, so there is still no silent downgrade. Constraints: no allocator for a per-entity options object, and QoS is a compile-time selection (RFC-0036/0045) so there is no runtime parameter machinery in the create path to read a value out of. A user loses re-tuning QoS by editing a YAML on the device; they re-run the plan instead.

cpp:ClockQoS.why: the clock preset (best-effort, keep-last(1)). OUR LANGUAGES DISAGREE: our C++ ships exactly THREE QoS presets -- `QoS::default_profile()`, `QoS::sensor_data()`, `QoS::services()` (qos.hpp) -- and C ships the same three as constants (`NROS_QOS_DEFAULT`, `NROS_QOS_SENSOR_DATA`, `NROS_QOS_SERVICES`), while Rust's `QosSettings` ships twelve: topics, sensor_data, services, parameters, parameter_events, clock, action_status, system, px4, plus the BEST_EFFORT/RELIABLE consts. So the profiles our OWN Rust parameter, clock and action code publishes on are unspellable from C and C++, and a ported node has to open a DDS reference and retype the numbers. Not a divergence -- nothing about a device stops a `constexpr QoS` named constructor from existing; the presets are just values. Phase 379 W3. Note the timer stage's `cpp:ClockQoS::ClockQoS` records only the type-per-preset SHAPE and reads as though we had the preset under another name; we do not.

cpp:DurabilityPolicy.why: rclcpp declares the four policy enums at namespace scope as `enum class`es. Ours are nested in `nros::QoS` and three of the four (`Reliability`, `Durability`, `History`) are PRIVATE; only `QoS::Liveliness` is public, and it is singular where rclcpp's is `LivelinessPolicy`. That is the same defect as the `_raw` getters and has the same fix -- see `cpp:QoS::reliability_raw`. One deliberate difference survives the rename: rclcpp's enums each carry `SystemDefault` and `Unknown`, which we decline. `SystemDefault` means defer to the middleware and there is none to defer to (RFC-0036, the backend is linked at build time); `Unknown` is a discovery artefact for a policy read off a remote endpoint, and we do no dynamic discovery.

cpp:KeepAll.why: a tag type whose only job is to feed rclcpp's `QoS(const QoSInitialization &, ...)` constructor with a history kind and depth. Ours sets the same two values with `QoS(int depth)` and the chainable `keep_last(n)` / `keep_all()` that rclcpp also has -- both already reconcile (`QoS::keep_last` is systematic, `QoS::keep_all` matches). So the values are reachable and only the construction SPELLING is gone: `rclcpp::QoS(rclcpp::KeepLast(10))` has to be ported to `nros::QoS(10)` or `nros::QoS().keep_last(10)`. Declined rather than added because a tag type per history kind exists to make an overload set resolve, and one constructor plus two setters resolves it with no types at all.

rust:QoSDuration.why: rclrs models every QoS duration as a tri-state enum -- `SystemDefault` (let the middleware pick), `Infinite`, `Custom(Duration)`. The `Infinite`/`Custom` split collapses into the sentinel, which costs the ability to express a genuinely zero window -- for deadline, lifespan and lease alike, zero and infinite both mean "do not enforce", so nothing is actually lost. The millisecond UNIT is the timer stage's rename (`rust:QoSProfile::deadline_duration`); this row is about the shape.

rust:QosOverride.why: ROS 2 implements `qos_overrides.<topic>.<role>.<policy>` launch parameters through the PARAMETER system at runtime: rclcpp's `QosOverridingOptions` declares them on the node and rebuilds the entity's profile from the declared values. Nothing here can do that -- entity QoS is compile-time (RFC-0036/0045) and there is no runtime parameter callback to rebuild an entity from. So the planner lowers the same launch parameter into a baked `&'static [QosOverride]` table and the entity folds the matching rows in at create time: one linear scan, no alloc, before the backend-compat check, so an override the active RMW cannot honour still errors loudly. rclrs has no QoS-override support at all.

rust:QosSettings::required_policies.why: backend-compatibility validation. Backends differ in which QoS policies they can honour at all -- zenoh-pico enforces no DEADLINE or LIFESPAN, XRCE none of the extended set -- so an entity requesting one the active backend cannot keep fails SYNCHRONOUSLY at create time with `TransportError::IncompatibleQos`, never a silent downgrade. ROS 2 answers the same question at runtime instead, through RxO matching and a QOS_INCOMPATIBLE event on the entity; both halves of that need dynamic discovery and the QoS event surface, and we have neither (see the qos stage's `c:get_zero_initialized_event`). `required_policies` reports what a profile asks for, `validate_against` checks it against what the session advertises.

rust:Session::next_deadline_ms.why: the backend's own next internal deadline (lease keepalive, heartbeat, ACK-NACK timeout), so the executor can cap its wait against it instead of waking early on a quiet link and round-tripping back into `drive_io`. See `rust:Session`.

rust:Session::supported_qos_policies.why: the RMW SEAM, one layer below the user API -- what a backend implements, not what a node calls; see `rust:Session::create_publisher` in the pubsub stage, and issue 0784 on `nros::` exporting the seam beside the API. rclrs has no equivalent because rcl is its only backend and DDS is assumed to honour every policy. It exists here because ours do not: zenoh-pico honours a different subset from Cyclone, and `QosSettings::validate_against` uses this mask to fail a create call with `INCOMPATIBLE_QOS` rather than downgrade silently (RFC-0036). OUR LANGUAGES DISAGREE: this is the only way in any of our three languages to ask which policies the linked backend honours, and it is Rust-only -- a C or C++ caller learns the answer only by getting `NROS_RET_INCOMPATIBLE_QOS` back from a create it already made. Same asymmetry as `Publisher::supports_event` in the pubsub stage.
